p: The hero's name means "exceedingly wise." Millard argued it can also mean "exceedingly devout."
b: The copies spell the name Atram-hasis, from atru, "surpassing," and hasis, "wise, attentive." Heidel explains it as "the exceedingly wise" and notes that it is a title more than a personal name. A. R. Millard pointed out that the root also covers care and devotion, so "the exceedingly devout" fits a man saved by obeying his god rather than by his own cleverness. In the Epic of Gilgamesh the same hero is Utnapishtim, and Ea says there that he let "Atrahasis" see a dream (Gilgamesh XI 187, as Millard cites it), so the two names belong to one figure. In the Sumerian Flood Story he is Ziusudra; in Berossus, Xisuthros.

p: Each Babylonian had a personal god. Atrahasis' god is Enki, and he calls himself Enki's servant.
b: "His lord" is Enki, the god of the fresh waters and of craft and cunning, whom Atrahasis serves (10:9 "his servant"). Babylonians spoke of "my god" as a personal patron who pleads for his worshiper among the great gods; Atrahasis will say "my god and your god" to the elders (10:35). The Old Babylonian Schøyen tablet, which seems to come just before this scene, shows Atrahasis kneeling before Ea in tears for the people, and Ea saying, "you are the one who reveres me." A Middle Babylonian copy from Ugarit has the hero say, "I am Atrahasis, an anointed priest; I live in the house of Ea my lord."

p: Atrahasis has had a dream and comes to his god to have it explained.
b: The column opens broken. When it resumes, Atrahasis is asking Enki to explain a dream (10:6-7), so the lost lines probably told of the dream itself. Tablet II ended with the gods' oath to bring the flood and Enki's refusal to take part (see chapter 9). In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Ea later defends himself by saying that he did not reveal the gods' secret but let Atrahasis see a dream (Gilgamesh XI 187, cited by Millard). Berossus also says the warning came in a dream, from the god he calls Kronos.

a: its head and search out its tail
p: A pair of opposites: "from beginning to end," the whole meaning of the dream.
b: Rēssa, "its head," and sibbassa, "its tail," are a merism, two ends standing for the whole, like English "from top to bottom." Atrahasis wants the dream's whole sense. In the Bible, Joseph and Daniel insist that the meaning of dreams belongs to God (Genesis 40:8; Daniel 2:27-28). Noah, by contrast, is never told anything by a dream: God speaks to him directly (Genesis 6:13).

p: The word is wardu, "slave, servant," the normal word for a worshiper before his god.
b: Ardu (older wardu) is the everyday word for a slave, and also the humble word a worshiper or an official uses for himself before a superior. Here it marks Atrahasis as Enki's devotee. The Bible uses the same kind of word (Hebrew eved) for God's chosen men: "my servant Moses," "my servant David," "my servant Job." Noah is never called God's servant; he is "righteous" and "walked with God" (Genesis 6:9).

a: Must I go searching in the bedroom?
p: Enki seems to answer an objection: the dream is not a riddle to be hunted for in the bedroom.
b: The line is hard. The first sign is damaged and SEAL corrects it to read uršu, "bedroom," the place where dreams come. Read that way, Enki quotes Atrahasis' worry ("Am I to search the bedroom for it?") and brushes it aside: listen instead to what I say now. Some take it as Enki's own rhetorical question. Either way the point is that the dream was only a cover; the real message is about to be spoken, though to a wall.

t: The god speaks to a wall
p: Enki is under oath not to tell a human. So he speaks to the reed wall, with Atrahasis behind it.
b: In chapter 9 the gods swore to bring the flood, and Enki was bound with them. He keeps the letter of the oath by talking to the wall of Atrahasis' reed house instead of to the man. The same trick appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh: Ea "repeated their speech to the reed hut: Reed hut, reed hut! Wall, wall!" (Gilgamesh XI 20-22), in the Middle Babylonian copy from Ugarit, and in the Ark Tablet. The Sumerian Flood Story already has Ziusudra standing by a wall at his left side when a voice speaks to him. Later the gods name the trick: "He let the word out through the reed wall" (12:40).

p: In southern Iraq people built houses of bundled reeds. A kikkišu is a reed fence or screen wall.
b: Kikkišu is a fence or screen of reeds, the light wall of a reed house such as the marsh people of southern Iraq still built in modern times. That Atrahasis lives in a reed house matters for the story: Enki tells him to leave it (10:15), and reeds also go into the boat (11:2 "the reed mats"; the Nippur copy says to build the boat of good reed).

p: The verb napādu is rare. SEAL glosses "separate, cut off"; Gilgamesh uses a different verb, "tear down."
b: The Old Babylonian line has upud bīta. SEAL's word list takes the verb as napādu, "to separate, cut off," so "depart from the house" or "leave the house behind." The Ark Tablet has the same words. The later Gilgamesh line has "Tear down the house" in Heidel's translation (Gilgamesh XI 24), as if the house's timber and reeds were to become the boat. The Plain keeps the Old Babylonian sense of leaving. Either way, everything Atrahasis owns is left behind.

t: Build a boat, make an ark
p: Enki's order sounds like Genesis 6:14. But Enki has to hide it; God gives it openly with a reason.
b: Agrees: in both stories a god warns one man and tells him to build a vessel to save life (Genesis 6:14, "Make yourself an ark of gopher wood."). Differs: Enki defies the other gods and whispers through a wall; in Genesis the one God who sends the flood is the God who warns, and he tells Noah why: "the earth is full of violence" (Genesis 6:13). Noah is not told to flee from a rival god but invited into a covenant (Genesis 6:18). The Bible's word for Noah's vessel, tevah, is used elsewhere only for the basket of baby Moses (Exodus 2:3); Atrahasis builds an eleppu, the ordinary word for a ship. This site keeps "boat" here and "ark" for Noah.

p: Enki's words sound like Jesus' call to let go of possessions to save one's life. The reasons differ.
b: Makkūra zēr-ma napišta bulliṭ, "hate property and keep life alive," became a fixed saying: Gilgamesh repeats it (Gilgamesh XI 25-26, Heidel). A Christian reader hears Jesus: "anyone who loses his life because of me will find it" and the warning about storing up treasure (Matthew 16:25-26; Luke 12:15-21; Luke 17:31-33, where Jesus tells those on the roof not to go down for their goods and to remember Lot's wife). Agrees: life is worth more than property in a day of judgment. Differs: Atrahasis saves his own life by a god's private tip; Jesus calls everyone, and the life he means is life with God.

p: Makkūru "possessions" and makūru "(god's) boat" sound almost alike. A wordplay may be intended.
b: This is Claude's suggestion. Enki says to reject makkūru, "possessions" (10:16). After the flood Enlil sees the makūru, the great boat (12:30, as SEAL's word list reads it). Babylonian poets loved puns on words that sound alike, and the poem plays on ṭēmu and eṭemmu in Tablet I. If the play is meant, the man who gave up his goods gained the boat that held life. Claude has not checked whether a published commentary makes this point; treat it as a possibility only. Jesus' saying fits the thought: "Anyone set on saving his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:25).

p: Napištu is the Akkadian cousin of Hebrew nefesh: throat, breath, life, a living being.
b: Napištu means the throat, then breath and life itself, like its Hebrew relative nefesh (Genesis 2:7 "a living being"). Bulliṭ is "make live, keep alive." Genesis uses the same idea for the ark: the animals come in "to be kept alive" (Genesis 6:19-20; 7:3). The Nippur copy gives the boat a name built on the same word: "Preserver of Life" (see the note at 10:18).

a: The boat that you will build
p: Here the lines break. Other copies describe a vessel quite unlike Noah's long box.
b: Only scraps survive: "equal" and "a circle" (10:19, 10:21). The Ark Tablet, published by Irving Finkel in 2014, fills in the plan: Enki draws it as a circle, with length and breadth equal, a floor of one ikû (a field measure) and walls one nindanu high, so a huge round coracle of rope and bitumen. The Middle Babylonian copy from Nippur calls it a great boat of good reed and gives it the name "Preserver of Life." In Gilgamesh its length and width are equal too (Gilgamesh XI 28-30), and it has six decks (XI 60). Genesis 6:15 alone gives a ship's proportions: 300 by 50 by 30 cubits (see the note on Genesis 6:15).

p: The Apsu is the fresh water under the earth, Enki's home, thought of as roofed over by the ground.
b: The Apsu was the great body of sweet water beneath the earth, from which springs and rivers rise, and Enki's own realm. It lay under the earth as under a roof, closed and dark. So the boat is to be sealed above and below like a world of water with a lid. Genesis has a related picture in "the springs of the great deep" (Genesis 7:11), but there the deep is not anyone's home; it is part of what God made and commands.

t: So the sun cannot see in
p: Shamash was the sun god and the judge who sees everything. The boat must be closed even to him.
b: Šamaš means "sun," and the sun god was the divine judge whose light sees every deed. A closed boat keeps out the rain, but the wording also hides the man from the all-seeing god, fitting the secret plan. Genesis says only "Give the ark a roof" (Genesis 6:16), and the one God of the Bible is never hidden from: "In every place the LORD has his eyes open" (Proverbs 15:3). In Gilgamesh, oddly, it is Shamash who sets the hour for the hero to go in (Gilgamesh XI 86). Noah is shut in by the LORD himself (Genesis 7:16), not hidden from him.

p: The Akkadian word for pitch, kupru, is the same word as the Hebrew kofer of Genesis 6:14.
b: Kupru is bitumen, the natural tar of Mesopotamia used to waterproof boats and baskets. Genesis 6:14 tells Noah to "coat it inside and outside with pitch," using the verb kafar and the noun kofer, the same word. The Ark Tablet spends many lines on the amounts of bitumen and the kilns that heated it.

a: a wealth of birds, bundles of fish
t: A promise with a hidden edge?
p: Enki promises "rain" of birds and fish. It sounds like plenty, but it may hint at the coming flood.
b: Enki says he will "rain down" birds and fish. On the surface it is a blessing, like food falling from the sky. Many readers see a double meaning: the rain will be the flood, and the "birds and fish" a picture of drowning. In Gilgamesh, Ea gives Utnapishtim words for the townspeople that work the same way: Ea will rain down plenty on them, birds and fish and a "wheat-rain" (Gilgamesh XI 43-47). If so, the god's promise is a riddle that saves one man and deceives the rest. Compare the manna and the quails that the LORD truly rains down to feed Israel (Exodus 16:4, 13; Psalm 78:24-27).

p: Enki sets a water clock running: the time left before the flood is measured out.
b: Maltaktu is a vessel used to measure time by water running out, a water clock (SEAL's word list gives "test, check; sand-clock"). Enki fills it and so starts a countdown. The Schøyen tablet says the gods fixed the flood for a set day, "by the day of the new moon." Genesis also gives Noah a countdown: "after seven more days I will bring rain" (Genesis 7:4), after the 120 years of Genesis 6:3 in the Jewish reading (see 10:32).

p: Atrahasis is told of seven nights; Noah is given seven days before the rain.
b: Seven marks the flood in nearly every telling. Here the flood will last seven nights, and it does (11:74 "Seven days and seven nights"). The Sumerian Flood Story has the same seven days and seven nights. In Genesis seven is the waiting time before the rain (Genesis 7:4, 10) and the pause between the birds (Genesis 8:10, 12), while the rain itself lasts forty days (Genesis 7:12). Genesis does not borrow the Babylonian timetable; its numbers make a full year in the ark (Genesis 7:11; 8:14).

a: He gathered the elders at his gate
t: A warning, or a cover story?
p: Atrahasis tells the elders he must leave because the gods quarrel. He does not warn them of the flood.
b: Atrahasis speaks to the town's leaders, but what he gives them is an excuse for leaving, not a warning (10:35-43). Utnapishtim is given nearly the same excuse in Gilgamesh (XI 35-42). Berossus has the same motif: the hero is told to say, if asked, that he is sailing "to the gods" to pray for good things for men. Differs: the New Testament calls Noah "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5), and says that by building the ark "he passed sentence on the world" (Hebrews 11:7). Jewish tradition says Noah worked on the ark for 120 years in the open, telling people that God was bringing a flood, so that they might repent (Genesis Rabbah 30:7; Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 108b). The Bible's God gives warning time; Enki's plan depends on silence.

p: Town elders met at the city gate. That Atrahasis can call them shows he is a man of rank.
b: In Babylonian towns, as in Israel, the elders were the heads of families who judged and decided at the gate (compare Ruth 4:1-2; Deuteronomy 21:19). Atrahasis summons them to his own gate. A. R. Millard took this as a sign of the hero's high standing, fitting the king of Shuruppak in the King List tradition and the priest of the Sumerian Flood Story and of the Ugarit copy. The Hattusa fragment also mentions "the assembly of the elders."

a: My god and your god do not agree
p: Atrahasis explains his leaving as a quarrel between his god Enki and the town's god Enlil.
b: The words are true in a way: Enki and Enlil are at odds over the flood. But Atrahasis says nothing of the danger. Each Babylonian city had its patron gods, and a man whose god had fallen out with the land's chief god might fear to stay. The scene shows the world of many gods at work: loyalty to one god can mean trouble with another. In the Bible there is no such rival to flee from: "the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39).

a: have grown angry with each other
p: SEAL's word list takes the verb as "stand," but its translation reads "became angry."
b: Itetezizū can be taken from ezēzu, "to be angry," in a form that means "kept being angry with each other," or from izuzzu, "to stand," which would give something like "have taken a stand (against each other)." SEAL's word list gives "to stand"; its English rendering has "became steadily angry." The Plain follows the sense of anger, which fits the next line: "They have driven me away."

a: Because I always stand in awe of Enki
p: Palāḫu is "to fear, revere." It is Atrahasis' piety that sets him apart.
b: The verb palāḫu covers fear and reverence, like Hebrew yare' in "the fear of the LORD." The form here means doing it again and again: Atrahasis is a man who habitually honors his god. Millard argued that this is why he is saved: "it was for his piety he was saved from destruction, just as Noah was saved for his righteousness." Berossus says Xisuthros was taken to live with the gods because of his reverence. Genesis gives the reason in its own terms: "Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes" and "was a righteous man" (Genesis 6:8-9).

p: In the lots of Tablet I, Enlil received the earth. To leave Enlil's ground is to leave the world.
b: At the start of the poem the gods cast lots: Anu took the sky, Enlil the earth, and Enki the Apsu (see 1:7-18). So "Enlil's ground" is all dry land. Atrahasis' cover story is that he will go down to Enki's realm, the waters. The irony is sharp: he will indeed live on the waters, in a boat, while Enlil's land is drowned. The Bible says rather "To the LORD belong the earth and all that fills it" (Psalm 24:1), and "To him belongs the sea" (Psalm 95:5).

a: I will go down to the Apsu with my god
t: Going down to the Apsu (Claude's theory)
p: The excuse may hide a truth: Atrahasis will live on the waters, Enki's realm, while the land drowns.
b: This is Claude's reading. Atrahasis' words are a cover story, but they come true in a hidden way: he goes onto the waters with his god's help and survives. The Ugarit copy has the hero say that he lives "in the house of Ea my lord," which fits a priest who serves at Enki's temple. Claude has not found this point in a published study; it is a reading of the irony, not a claim about the poet's intent. A Christian reader may compare the double meaning in 1 Peter 3:20-21, where the same water that judges the world carries Noah's family safe.

p: Carpenter, reed worker, rich and poor: everyone brings something to the boat, not knowing why.
b: The list shows a whole community at work: the carpenter with his axe, the reed worker with his stone (perhaps for beating reeds), the rich man with costly bitumen, the poor man with what he could. Gilgamesh tells the same scene at greater length: "The child brought pitch" (Gilgamesh XI 54). The townspeople build the vessel that will save one family and not themselves. Jewish tradition tells instead of people mocking Noah as he built (Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 108b), and Jesus speaks of people going about their lives until the day Noah went in (Matthew 24:38-39).

a: Whatever silver he had, he loaded on it
p: After rejecting possessions, Atrahasis loads his silver and gold. Noah takes only family, animals and food.
b: These lines are mostly restored from the matching passage in Gilgamesh, where Utnapishtim loads all his silver, all his gold and "the seed of all living creatures" (Gilgamesh XI 81-83, Heidel). It sits oddly beside Enki's command to reject possessions (10:16). Differs: Genesis lists only Noah's family, the animals and "some of every food that is eaten" (Genesis 6:21). There is no treasure in the ark, and no craftsmen; the new world begins with nothing but life.

p: The oxen are ellu, "pure, clean." Genesis also speaks of clean animals, but for a different use.
b: Ellu is "pure, clean," the word for what is fit for the gods. Atrahasis slaughters clean oxen and fat sheep, apparently for the farewell feast (10:67-68). Genesis is the only other flood story with clean animals: Noah takes "seven and seven" of every clean animal (Genesis 7:2), and after the flood he offers them on the altar (Genesis 8:20). Agrees: the line between clean and other animals is older than the Law of Moses. Differs: in Genesis the clean animals are saved for worship after the rescue; here they are eaten before it.

a: the winged birds of the sky
p: Birds, herds and wild creatures go into the boat, as in Genesis 6:19-20 and 7:14.
b: The list of birds, herds and wild animals is close to Genesis: "From the birds by their kind, from the herd animals by their kind" (Genesis 6:20). The Old Babylonian copy says nothing of pairs. The Ark Tablet does: wild animals "two by two" go into the boat (see the variant at 10:64). Differs: Genesis repeats "male and female" and "by their kind" because the point is that every kind will live on and fill the earth again (Genesis 7:3; 8:17).

p: SEAL reads "craftsmen" here, with a question mark. Gilgamesh lists craftsmen in its boat too.
b: The broken start of the line is read by SEAL as mārī ummâni, "craftsmen" (literally "sons of the craftsman"), but marked uncertain, so the Plain leaves it out. Gilgamesh has Utnapishtim take "all the craftsmen" on board (XI 85), and in Babylonian tradition the sages who brought arts and skills to humankind belonged to the world before the flood. Genesis has only eight people in the ark (Genesis 7:13; 1 Peter 3:20).

t: Eating and drinking before the flood
p: A feast before the flood: Jesus says people were eating and drinking until Noah went into the ark.
b: Atrahasis gives a banquet for his people, and "the eater ate; the drinker drank" (10:70-71), while the guests know nothing of what is coming. The Ark Tablet has the same line. Jesus uses the same picture for the days before his coming: "Before the flood came, people went on eating and drinking ... until the very day Noah went into the ark" (Matthew 24:38). Genesis itself has no feast. There is no sign that Jesus knew this poem; the shared picture is of ordinary life going on, unaware, until judgment comes.

p: Atrahasis puts his family aboard. Genesis names them: Noah, his wife, three sons and their wives.
b: Kimtu is the family or clan. The Ark Tablet adds in-laws and pregnant women, and the Nippur copy has "bring up your family and your kin." Genesis counts exactly: Noah, his wife, Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives (Genesis 7:13), "eight souls" in 1 Peter 3:20. In Genesis the family is saved for Noah's sake: "you and your whole house, because you are the one I have seen to be righteous" (Genesis 7:1).

a: He could not sit down; he could not kneel
p: Atrahasis is sick with grief and fear as the guests feast. Genesis says nothing of Noah's feelings.
b: Atrahasis paces in and out, unable to sit or kneel, "his heart broken," vomiting bile (10:74). He knows what his guests do not. The poet gives his hero a real inner life, a burden of knowing that most will die. Genesis is silent about Noah's feelings; it says only that "Noah did everything the LORD commanded him" (Genesis 7:5). Ezekiel later names Noah with Daniel and Job as men whose righteousness could save only themselves (Ezekiel 14:14), and Abraham shows the grief that pleads for a city (Genesis 18:23-32).

a: The face of the day changed
p: Literally "the day changed its face": the weather turned.
b: Ūmu išnû pānūšu, "the day changed its face," means the sky darkened and the weather turned. Jesus uses the same picture: "You can tell what the face of the sky means" (Matthew 16:3). Gilgamesh has a black cloud rising from the horizon at dawn, with Adad thundering in it (XI 97-98).

p: Adad was the god of storms and rain, the Mesopotamian form of the storm god the Bible calls Baal or Hadad.
b: Adad thunders in the clouds as the flood begins. He is the same storm god known in Syria as Hadad and in Canaan as Baal, "the rider on the clouds." The Bible answers that thunder and flood belong to the LORD: "At the Flood the LORD took his throne; / the LORD sits as King forever" (Psalm 29:10), at the end of a psalm that hands every thunderclap to the LORD (Psalm 29:3-9). Names with Hadad appear for Syrian kings (Ben-hadad, 1 Kings 15:18).

p: The god's "noise" is rigmu, the same word for the human noise that Enlil could not stand.
b: Rigmu is the word the poem used for the din of humankind that robbed Enlil of sleep (see 5:2-8 and chapter 6). Now it is the god's noise, the thunder, that fills the world, and soon "the noise of the flood" frightens the gods themselves (11:18, 11:21). Nintu will say the human noise has "gone still" (11:45). The poet seems to be paying the gods back in their own coin. In Genesis the sin is not noise but violence (Genesis 6:11-13), and the "outcry" God hears in Scripture is usually the cry of the wronged (Genesis 4:10; 18:20-21).

p: Atrahasis seals his own door with pitch. In Genesis, "the LORD shut the door behind him."
b: Atrahasis bolts and seals his door himself; Utnapishtim does the same in Gilgamesh (XI 93), and in the Ark Tablet the hero gives the order to seal it. Genesis 7:16 says, "Then the LORD shut the door behind him" (vayyisgor YHWH ba'ado). Differs: the biblical God keeps Noah safe with his own hand; the Babylonian hero has to protect himself, even from the gods. Augustine saw in the ark's single door in its side a figure of Christ's pierced side, through which people enter the church (City of God 15.26); compare Jesus' "I am the door" (John 10:9).

p: The wind snaps the rope that tied the boat to land. From now on it drifts.
b: Markasu is a rope or tie, here the mooring line. The wind "cut" it and "released" the boat. The picture is of a vessel with no rudder, carried by the storm, as the ark "drifted on the face of the waters" (Genesis 7:18). The Ark Tablet's round coracle and Noah's box-shaped ark were both built to float, not to sail.

p: Burû is a reed mat. Reed mats may have lined or covered the boat.
b: The column opens with only a few words. Burû, "reed mat," is the woven matting used for floors, roofs and boat covers in the marshes. The Ark Tablet builds its boat of rope coiled and coated with bitumen, and the Nippur copy says to build it of good reed. The mats here may be the boat's covering against the rain.

p: A creature with talons tears the sky. SEAL suggests the storm bird Anzu, but the name is lost.
b: The subject of these lines is broken away. SEAL's translation restores, with a question mark, Anzu, the lion-headed storm bird of Mesopotamian myth, whose talons fit ṣupru, "claw." The picture is of the storm as a monster tearing the sky open. Genesis says plainly "the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11), not by a monster but by God, who made the sky and its waters (Genesis 1:6-8).

t: The noise smashed like a pot
p: The land's "noise" is broken like clay. The flood finally silences the human din.
b: Rigimša iḫpi, "he broke its noise," with "like a clay pot" restored from the matching line of Gilgamesh, where the storm god "broke the land like a pot" (Heidel). In Atrahasis it is the land's noise that is shattered, the very thing that disturbed Enlil (see 10:77). The Bible uses the broken pot for judgment too, but on sin, not on noise: "you will shatter them like a jar from the potter" (Psalm 2:9; compare Jeremiah 19:10-11).

p: Kašūšu is a divine weapon, then "annihilation": the flood comes on like an army.
b: SEAL's word list gives kašūšu as "annihilation, crushing defeat"; the gloss in the score calls it a divine weapon. The flood moves over people "like a battle," a picture repeated in Gilgamesh: "Like a battle it came over the people" (Heidel). The Bible also pictures God's judgment as a flood that sweeps like an army (Isaiah 8:7-8; Daniel 9:26), but promises that "the waters of Noah" will not come again (Isaiah 54:9).

a: A brother could not see his brother
t: Darkness where no one sees his brother
p: The same words as the plague of darkness in Egypt: "A man could not see his brother."
b: Ul īmur aḫu aḫašu, "a brother did not see his brother," is matched word for word by Exodus 10:23, lo ra'u ish et-achiv: "A man could not see his brother." Gilgamesh has "No man could see his fellow" (Heidel). It was an idiom for total darkness, shared by the languages of the region. The likeness shows a common world of speech, not borrowing. In Exodus the next words make the point: "But for all the Israelites there was light in their homes." God's darkness distinguishes; Enlil's flood does not (see 12:50).

p: Karāšu is a key word of the flood: "catastrophe, annihilation." It recurs in 11:52, 12:16, 12:35 and 12:94.
b: Karāšu is the word the poem uses for the destruction of humankind in the flood. The gods "rounded up the people for disaster" (11:52; 12:16); Enlil asks how a man lived through "the disaster" (12:35), and the closing hymn says the same (12:94). Gilgamesh uses the same word: "No man was meant to survive the destruction" (Thompson's text has ina karāši). The Plain keeps "disaster" each time so the thread shows.

p: Darkness with no sun: the prophets describe the Day of the LORD the same way.
b: Šamaš laššu, "Shamash is not there": the sun, and the sun god, are gone. The prophets describe God's day of judgment in the same colors: "Will the day of the LORD not be dark and not bright" (Amos 5:20); "A day of darkness and gloom" (Joel 2:2). Genesis does not describe the darkness of the flood at all; it counts days and months (Genesis 7:11-24).

p: The drowned people are like flies on the water. Flies return as a picture three more times.
b: Flies run through the end of the poem: the dead float like flies (11:17), Nintu laments that her offspring "have become" like flies (11:42-43), the hungry gods crowd "like flies" over the offering (12:8), and Nintu takes "these flies" as the lapis lazuli of her necklace (12:27-28). The picture ties the dead humans, the greedy gods and the goddess's memorial together. The fly also stands for the worthless in the Bible (Ecclesiastes 10:1; Isaiah 7:18), and "Baal-zebub," "lord of flies," is the god of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2).

a: The gods feared the noise of the flood
t: Gods afraid of their own flood
p: The gods who sent the flood flee from it in fear. The God of Genesis is never afraid of the waters.
b: The gods decreed the flood but cannot control it. They run up to the sky and huddle there; Gilgamesh says they "cowered like dogs" (Heidel). Differs: in the Bible the LORD rules the flood: "At the Flood the LORD took his throne; / the LORD sits as King forever" (Psalm 29:10). God "remembered Noah" and "made a wind blow over the earth, and the waters calmed" (Genesis 8:1). Jesus stills the storm with a word, and his disciples ask, "Who can this be?" (Mark 4:39-41).

p: Ṭēmu, "understanding, plan, decision," is the word Anu is lord of. Here it fails him.
b: Ṭēmu covers understanding, good sense, a plan and a decision. Anu is called "the lord of understanding" (11:49; 12:13), the one who makes decisions for the gods. Now his ṭēmu "changed": he is beside himself. The same word sounds in the making of humankind, where the slain god "who had understanding" gives humans their spirit (see chapter 3). The Bible says God's understanding has no limit (Isaiah 40:28; Psalm 147:5).

p: The mother goddess has several names. The tablet calls her Nintu here and Mami in 11:31.
b: The goddess who made humankind from clay in Tablet I has several names: Nintu, "lady of birth"; Mami or Mama, "mother"; and the title Belet-ili, "mistress of the gods," which the gods gave her after she made humankind. The Plain keeps the name each line uses: Nintu here, "the wise Mami" in 11:31. In Gilgamesh her part is taken by Belet-ili, called "Ishtar" in one line (Heidel).

p: With no one left to bring offerings, the gods go hungry. The Bible's God needs nothing from humans.
b: Humankind was made to feed the gods by its labor (Tablet I). Now the gods have drowned their own servants and sit hungry and thirsty. This is the heart of the poem's theology: gods and humans need each other. Conflicts: the Bible denies that God depends on offerings: "Suppose I were hungry: I would not say so to you, / for the world and everything in it is mine" (Psalm 50:12). Paul tells the Athenians that God is not served by human hands "as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25). Moses mocks the gods "who ate the fat of their sacrifices" but cannot help (Deuteronomy 32:37-38).

a: The goddess saw it and wept
t: A grieving mother goddess, a grieving God
p: Nintu weeps for the humans she made. Genesis says the LORD was pained to his heart before the flood.
b: Nintu grieves after the flood has started, for the children she helped to destroy. Agrees: the Bible also speaks of God's grief over humankind: "it pained him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6). Differs: the LORD grieves before the flood, over evil, and acts with justice and mercy; Nintu grieves after it, over her own part in a decision she now calls wrong (11:34-37). God does not regret the judgment as a mistake; after it he binds himself by a covenant never to send such a flood again (Genesis 9:11).

p: Mami is the divine midwife: she shaped humankind and helped bring them to birth in Tablet I.
b: Tabsūt ili, "midwife of the gods," recalls Tablet I, where Mami mixed clay with a god's flesh and blood and, with the birth goddesses, brought the first humans to birth. So her grief here is a mother's grief. The Bible gives the life-giving title to a woman, not a goddess: Eve, "because she was the mother of everyone living" (Genesis 3:20).

p: Nintu blames herself for agreeing to the flood in the assembly, and blames Enlil for forcing her.
b: Nintu says she spoke for "total destruction" in the assembly along with the other gods, then says Enlil pushed her to it. Scholars read the speech as the poem's own judgment on the flood: even the gods who voted for it call it wrong. Gilgamesh gives the same lament to Belet-ili: "How could I command (such) evil in the assembly of the gods!" (Heidel). A Christian reader notices a council that can make a terrible mistake, then regret it. Scripture says the LORD's counsel stands, and that his judgments are true and just (Psalm 33:11; Revelation 16:7).

p: A name that appears only here. No one knows who Tiruru was.
b: SEAL lists Tiruru as the name of a god, and nothing more is known. The line seems to compare Enlil's pressure on Nintu to something Tiruru did: twisting or confusing someone's words. The verb in 11:39 is also uncertain (SEAL corrects one sign). The Plain keeps the name and the plain sense, "he twisted my words."

a: I heard their noise come upon me
p: Either she listened to Enlil's complaint about human noise, or she now hears the dying cries.
b: The two lines are hard. SEAL's translation reads them as a confession: against her own nature she listened to Enlil's case against human noise. Read more literally, ina ṣērīya ... rigimšina ešme says "upon me I heard their noise," which may mean she now hears the cries of the drowning. Either way the word is rigmu again, the noise that started everything (see 10:77). Genesis says God heard a different sound: the blood of Abel crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10), the outcry of Sodom's victims (Genesis 18:20-21).

p: Lillidu means "offspring." Nintu speaks of humankind as her own children.
b: Lillidu is "offspring, young." Nintu calls humans her own brood, because she shaped them. The line "Above me, like flies, / the offspring have become" is hard: elēnuya means "above me," but some take it as "beyond me" or "without me." Gilgamesh gives Belet-ili a related line: "For it is I who bring forth these my people! Like the spawn of fish they now fill the sea" (Heidel).

p: Heaven has become a house of mourning where the human noise is silent.
b: Nintu compares her dwelling to a bīt dimmati, a house of moaning, where the noise has gone "deathly still" (šaḫurru). The noise Enlil wanted silenced is silenced, and the result is not rest but grief. Ecclesiastes uses the house of mourning as the place where the living learn wisdom (Ecclesiastes 7:2, 4). Jesus promises that those who mourn will be comforted (Matthew 5:4), and Revelation that God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

p: Nintu went up to the sky, but finds it like living in a storehouse: closed, dark and cut off.
b: Bīt nakmati is a treasury or storehouse. SEAL takes the lines as "It is as if I were dwelling in a treasure house." Some readers hear a bitter joke: the storeroom is empty, now that no offerings come. Others take it as a place shut up and airless. Either way heaven has become a prison for the goddess. In the Bible God's "storehouses" hold snow, hail and wind for his purposes (Job 38:22; Psalm 135:7).

p: Nintu blames Anu, the chief god, for letting his sons bring the flood without counsel.
b: Anu is the father of the gods and the head of their assembly. Bēl ṭēmi, "lord of understanding" or "lord of decision," is an ironic title here: his understanding has just failed (11:23). Nintu's charge is that the gods "did not think it through" (lā imtalkū), the same accusation she makes against Enlil after the flood (12:15) and Enki makes too (12:46). Belet-ili says the same in Gilgamesh: Enlil "did not reflect but brought on the flood" (Thompson). The poem's gods can act without wisdom. Isaiah says the LORD's counsel is wonderful and his wisdom great (Isaiah 28:29).

a: If only the father had given birth to my people!
p: Nintu may wish that the father of the gods had borne humankind, and so bore the blame.
b: The line is unclear. Abu-mān ulda seems to mean "would that a father had borne," so Nintu may wish that Anu, "the father," had been humankind's maker, so that she would not have to watch her own children die. Others read abu differently. The Bible does call God both Father and the one who gives birth (Deuteronomy 32:18; Isaiah 66:13), but God does not wish he had not made his children; he sends his Son to save them (John 3:16).

p: The drowned float on the sea like dragonflies on a river: light, many and lifeless.
b: Kulīlu is the dragonfly. Here the swarm of insects on the water is the dead of the flood. In Gilgamesh XI Belet-ili uses "the spawn of fish" instead (Heidel). The Bible's image for the shortness of life is grass and its flower (Isaiah 40:6-8; Psalm 103:15-16).

p: The dead drift like rafts and come to rest against the marsh and the river bank.
b: Amu is a raft. The bodies of the drowned pile up where the water leaves them, against the meadows and the banks. The picture is stark and real; flood victims in the river plains of Mesopotamia ended like this. Genesis states the same fact without images: "All flesh that moved on the earth died" (Genesis 7:21).

p: Unappiš is literally "made wide, let breathe": weeping eased her heart. Enki uses the same verb in 12:48.
b: Libbaša unappiš: the verb napāšu means "to breathe," and in this form "to let breathe, make roomy." Weeping relieves her tight heart. Enki later urges Enlil to do the same (12:48), and someone says "I have let my heart breathe" in 12:56. The Plain keeps one English phrase for all three so the echo shows. Lamentations likewise urges grieving Zion to pour out her heart like water before the Lord (Lamentations 2:19).

p: Beer was one of the gods' daily offerings. With no offerings, the goddess thirsts.
b: Temples served the gods meals each day: bread, meat, beer and wine, set before the statue. The grieving goddess thirsts for the beer that humans used to pour. The detail is not comic in the poem; it shows how the gods' life hung on human work. Israel also poured drink offerings (Numbers 15:5-10), but the Law presents them as gifts to God, not his food: "Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls?" (Psalm 50:13).

t: Gods like sheep at a trough
p: The great gods crowd like thirsty sheep around a trough. The poet makes them look small.
b: The Anunnaki, "the great gods" of 11:28, now jostle like sheep at a water trough (rāṭu, a channel or pipe). Gilgamesh uses an even lower picture: the gods "cowered like dogs." The poet does not mock the gods outright, but shows them helpless. A Christian reader may recall the prophets' plain words about idols that must be carried because they cannot walk (Jeremiah 10:5; Isaiah 46:1-2). Psalm 23 turns the sheep image the other way: the LORD is the shepherd who leads his flock to water.

p: Seven days and nights here and in the Sumerian story; a year, with forty days of rain, in Genesis.
b: The storm lasts seven days and seven nights, as the water clock promised (10:29-30). The Sumerian Flood Story has the same; Gilgamesh has six days and six nights, with calm on the seventh, in Heidel's translation. Genesis has forty days of rain (Genesis 7:12), 150 days of high water (Genesis 7:24) and about a year in the ark (Genesis 7:11; 8:14). Differs: the biblical flood is longer and more ordered, with dates like a ship's log, which Millard took as one reason to prefer it as history.

a: (At least sixteen lines are lost or too broken to read.)
p: The end of the flood is lost: the boat's landing and, if this version had it, the sending of the birds.
b: Between the storm and the offering (12:3-4) the tablet is broken for many lines. In Gilgamesh this is where the boat grounds on a mountain and the hero sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven (Gilgamesh XI; see the note on Genesis 8:8). Millard noted that the bird episode "is not present" in what survives of Atrahasis, but that the manuscript is broken at that point, so it may once have been there. Berossus also has birds sent out three times.

a: (Only the first signs of a word survive.)
p: SEAL's word list reads the broken word as ittu, "sign." Too little survives to build on it.
b: SEAL lemmatizes the two surviving signs it-t[a ...] as ittu, "sign, omen." It is tempting to connect a "sign" near the end of the flood with the bow that God sets in the clouds as "the sign of a covenant" (Genesis 9:13). But two signs could begin many words, and nothing around them survives. This is Claude's note of caution, not a claim: the line should not be used as evidence of a Babylonian "sign" after the flood.

a: (About twenty-eight lines are lost or too broken to read.)
p: The top of the column is gone. When it resumes, Atrahasis is making an offering.
b: Some twenty-eight lines are missing or too broken for translation. They must have told how the waters went down and how Atrahasis left the boat. In Gilgamesh this is where the boat rests on Mount Nimush, the birds are sent out and the hero brings everything out "to the four winds" before he sacrifices (Thompson's text). Genesis has the ark rest "on the mountains of Ararat" (Genesis 8:4).

t: The first act after the flood
p: Atrahasis' first act is an offering, as Noah's is. But the meaning of the offering differs.
b: "To the four winds," restored from Gilgamesh, means in every direction, to all the gods. Agrees: Genesis too makes worship the first act of the new world: "Noah built an altar to the LORD" and offered clean animals and birds (Genesis 8:20). Berossus likewise has Xisuthros build an altar. Differs: Atrahasis feeds many hungry gods; Noah honors one God who needs nothing (see the note at 11:29), and the LORD answers with a promise for the whole earth (Genesis 8:21-22).

p: Niqû is the common word for a sacrifice or poured offering. The verb naqû means to pour out.
b: Ittaqi niqâ, "he poured an offering": naqû is to pour a libation, and niqû is any offering, often an animal sacrifice. Noah's offering is olah, a whole burnt offering, where the whole animal goes up in smoke to God (Genesis 8:20; Leviticus 1). In Atrahasis the gods "ate the offering" (12:9); in the Law the burnt offering is not food for God but "a soothing smell" (Leviticus 1:9).

p: The gods smell the offering. Genesis says "The LORD smelled the soothing smell": a deliberate echo or a shared idiom.
b: Iṣinū ilū erēša, "the gods smelled the scent," restored from Gilgamesh, where the line comes twice. Genesis 8:21 says "The LORD smelled the soothing smell" (vayyarach YHWH et-reach hannichoach). This is one of the closest verbal links between the two flood stories (see the note on Genesis 8:21). Differs: the gods crowd in to eat because they are starving; the LORD, smelling the offering, speaks "in his heart" a promise never again to strike every living thing. Paul reads the phrase forward to Christ, who handed himself over "as an offering and a sacrifice to God, a soothing smell" (Ephesians 5:2).

a: When they had eaten the offering
p: The gods eat the offering. The Bible's God does not eat, and mocks gods that "ate the fat of their sacrifices."
b: Atrahasis says outright that the gods "ate" the offering. That fits the Babylonian temple, where meals were set before the god's statue each day. Conflicts: Scripture denies that God eats: "Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls?" (Psalm 50:13). The Greek addition to Daniel, Bel and the Dragon, tells of priests who secretly ate the food set before Bel. Moses asks where the gods are now, "who ate the fat of their sacrifices" (Deuteronomy 32:38).

p: Nintu turns on all the gods, and then on Enlil, for the flood.
b: The goddess who made humankind speaks for them. She repeats her earlier charge (11:49-52) and singles out Enlil: he comes to the incense but did not think before he brought the flood. In Gilgamesh Belet-ili goes further and says Enlil should not come to the offering at all (Thompson). Scholars note that the poem lets its own gods judge the flood as rash. The Bible's verdict on the flood is the reverse: it was just, because "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:11), and God's grief came before it, not after it.

p: Qutrēnu is incense smoke. Enlil, who sent the flood, now draws near to enjoy the smoke.
b: Qutrēnu is incense or fragrant smoke, part of Babylonian offerings. Israel burned incense too, on a gold altar before the LORD (Exodus 30:1-10), and the psalmist prays, "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you" (Psalm 141:2). The irony is Nintu's: the god who wanted humans silenced comes running to their smoke.

a: their bright faces have gone dark
p: The once-bright faces of humankind are darkened in death.
b: Ellūtum zīmūšina, "their pure faces," have "gone dark" (i'adrū). The faces may be the drowned humans', or the faces of the goddesses, darkened by grief. Either way light gives way to gloom, as in 11:32-33. The Bible uses a shining face for God's favor: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you" in the priestly blessing (Numbers 6:25).

p: The "big flies" seem to be beads of a necklace that Anu had made for the goddess.
b: Nintu goes to "the big flies that Anu had hung up long before." The next lines make the flies the lapis lazuli of her neck (12:27-28). In Gilgamesh the goddess lifts up "the great jewels which Anu had made" and swears by the lapis lazuli on her neck that she will never forget these days (Gilgamesh XI, Heidel). So the dead, who floated like flies (11:17), become the beads of her memorial necklace.

p: Two words here are corrected by the editors. "Long before" could also be "in front of the gods of old."
b: The tablet's signs are confused here, and SEAL marks corrections on two words (see the variant). Ina pān qadmi can mean "in former time" (so the Plain, "long before") or "in front of the ancient one(s)," and SEAL's English has "in front of the gods." The point is that Anu once gave the goddess this necklace.

a: The grief for them is mine!
t: A god who owns the grief
p: Nintu claims the grief as her own lot. The Bible shows a God who grieves, and then acts to save.
b: Yâttum nissassunu: "mine is the wailing for them." Nintu takes the grief as her destiny (šīmtu, 12:22). Agrees: Scripture also speaks of God's pain over humankind (Genesis 6:6) and his compassion like a mother's: "Can a woman forget her nursing baby ... but as for me, I will never forget you" (Isaiah 49:15). Differs: Nintu's grief changes nothing for the dead; she can only remember. The God of the Bible grieves and also rules, promises and saves, and in Christ bears the grief himself (Isaiah 53:4).

a: must be the lapis lazuli of my neck
t: A necklace to remember, a bow to remember
p: The goddess's necklace makes her remember the flood. In Genesis God sets his bow in the clouds and remembers.
b: Nintu makes the flies her necklace "so that I may remember the days" (12:29). Many readers set this beside Genesis 9:13-16: "my bow I have put in the clouds" and "I will see it and remember the covenant." Agrees: both stories end with a visible sign hung up in heaven's sight, tied to remembering the flood. Differs: the necklace keeps a goddess's grief alive; the bow keeps a promise to every living creature. Nintu remembers the dead; God remembers his covenant with the living, "and the waters will never again become a flood to ruin all flesh" (Genesis 9:15). Whether Genesis is answering this picture is debated; the link is in the theme, not the words.

a: so that I may remember the days
p: The goddess swears to keep the flood days in mind, like the gods' oath in Gilgamesh.
b: Luḫsus, "may I remember," from ḫasāsu. The line breaks off. Gilgamesh has the full oath: "I shall remember these days and shall not forget them ever" (Heidel). In Genesis the remembering is God's: "God remembered Noah" (Genesis 8:1) and "I will remember my covenant" (Genesis 9:15). In Hebrew "remember" (zakhar) means to act on behalf of someone, not just to recall.

p: Here the boat is makūru, a word for a god's processional barge, not eleppu as before.
b: SEAL's word list takes ma-ku-ra as makūru, a large boat of the kind used to carry a god's statue in procession, not the everyday eleppu of 10:15. The Nippur copy also calls the vessel by a related name, makurkurru, "Preserver of Life." Enlil sees a grand vessel where he expected no survivors. The word sounds almost the same as makkūru, "possessions," which Atrahasis was told to reject in 10:16; see the spec note there.

t: Who is Enlil, and the God of the Bible?
p: Enlil sends the flood; the Bible's one God sends the flood too. Is Enlil a bent memory of God?
b: Enlil, "Lord Wind," was king of the gods at Nippur, the god who rules the earth and gives the gods' decisions force. He sends the flood, as the LORD does in Genesis. What fits: both are the high ruler whose decree brings the flood. What does not: Enlil acts from irritation at noise, "without thinking" (12:15), is outwitted by Enki and furious that anyone lived; the LORD acts from grief at evil, saves Noah himself and makes a covenant. Some Christian readers, such as A. R. Millard, think both stories remember one real flood, which the Babylonians "could only conceive ... in their own polytheistic language." Verdict: Enlil is not the God of the Bible; at most his role in the story is a distorted memory of the judge of the earth.

a: he was full of fury at the Igigi
p: Enlil blames the Igigi, the younger gods, for the leak. Anu points to Enki instead.
b: In Tablet I the Igigi were the gods who did the labor and rebelled (see chapter 2). Enlil's first suspicion falls on them. Gilgamesh has the same line: Enlil "was filled with anger against the Igigi" (Thompson). The scene shows a heaven of suspicion and quarrels. The Bible's heavenly court has a different tone: angels who do God's will (Psalm 103:20-21), and angels who sinned, whom God judges (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). On whether the rebel gods of this poem answer to the Watchers of 1 Enoch, see chapter 2.

p: The gods bound themselves by an oath to destroy humankind. Enki got around it by speaking to a wall.
b: Māmītu is an oath sworn under a curse. All the great gods had "put their mouths" to it (chapter 9). Enki kept the words but broke the spirit, speaking to a wall (10:13). The Bible also has God binding himself by oath, but in the other direction: "as I swore that Noah's waters / would never again sweep over the earth" (Isaiah 54:9). God swears to save, and he keeps his word (Hebrews 6:17-18).

a: Where did the secret get out?
p: The gods' decision was a secret. Jewish writings also tell of a secret revealed to Noah.
b: Pirištu is a secret, the hidden decision of the gods. In Gilgamesh the whole flood story is told as "a secret of the gods." Jewish writers before Jesus also tell of heaven sending word to Noah: in 1 Enoch an angel is sent to the son of Lamech to say, "Hide yourself" and to teach him how to escape (1 Enoch 10:1-3), and in the Animal Vision one of the four heavenly beings "taught him a secret" before he built his boat (1 Enoch 89:1). Differs from Genesis: there God speaks to Noah directly and openly, and the New Testament calls Noah a herald (2 Peter 2:5). Amos says "The Lord GOD does nothing at all / unless he has shown his secret counsel / to his servants the prophets" (Amos 3:7).

a: How did a man live through the disaster?
p: Enlil is angry that a man survived. In Genesis God himself keeps Noah alive.
b: Enlil had meant no one to live. Genesis turns the whole story on the one who lives: "Only Noah remained, with whoever was with him in the ark" (Genesis 7:23). Differs: in Genesis the survival is God's purpose from the start (Genesis 6:8, 18); here it is Enki's trick against the other gods. The New Testament makes the few saved through water a picture of salvation: "a few, eight souls, were carried safe through water" (1 Peter 3:20).

t: Enki and the God who warns Noah
p: Enki warns and saves the hero. Is Enki a memory of the God who warned Noah?
b: Enki (Ea) is the god of fresh water, wisdom and craft, the friend of humankind who made them with Mami and saves them from plague, drought and flood. What fits: like the LORD in Genesis 6:13-21 he warns one man, tells him to build a vessel and gives its plan. What does not: Enki works against the other gods and by deceit; he swore to the flood with them; he does not judge evil. In Genesis the God who warns is the same God who judges, so there is no split between justice and mercy. Verdict: unlikely to be "the same being"; the two roles the Bible joins in one God are split here between Enlil and Enki. In Gilgamesh it is Ninurta who names Ea as the culprit.

a: Yes, I did it, right in front of you!
p: Enki admits what he did and defends it: he kept life safe.
b: Enki does not deny the act. His defense is that he "kept life safe" (uštaṣṣira napištam) and that Enlil acted without thinking. In Gilgamesh, Ea is slyer: he says he did not reveal the secret but let the wise man see a dream. Readers have long seen Enki as the trickster friend of humans. A Christian reader notes that the Bible never needs a god to outwit God for people to be saved; the rescue comes from God's own will (Genesis 6:8; 1 Timothy 2:4).

a: pull the rope tight, then let it go slack
p: A saying about rule: tighten and loosen. Punish, but not to the point of destruction.
b: SEAL's translation marks this as a saying: "pull tight, then slack," like handling a rope or a bow. The restored first word is from SEAL. Gilgamesh has Ea say the same in the next lines; Heidel's note gives the sense: punish man lest he get too wild, but not too severely, lest he perish. The Bible speaks of God's discipline as fair and limited: "I will discipline you fairly" (Jeremiah 30:11), and "He will not go on accusing without end" (Psalm 103:9).

a: Lay your punishment on the one who is guilty
p: Enki's rule is the Bible's too: punish the one who sinned, not the whole world.
b: [Bēl ar]nim šukun šērētka, "on the owner of the guilt put your punishment." Gilgamesh has the famous form: "On the sinner lay his sin, on the transgressor lay his transgression" (Thompson). When Millard wrote in 1967 that line was not yet known in Atrahasis; this column now preserves a command to the same effect. Agrees: Abraham makes the same appeal: "putting the righteous to death with the wicked ... Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25), and Ezekiel: "The person who sins, that very person will die" (Ezekiel 18:20). Differs: in Genesis the flood is itself that justice, with the righteous man spared; here Enki accuses the chief god of killing the innocent with the guilty, which Heidel saw as the deepest moral gap between the stories.

p: Šassūru means "womb" and is a title of the mother goddess. The Plain calls her "the birth goddess."
b: Šassūru (here spelled sassūru) is literally "womb," and as a title it names the mother goddess as the power of birth. In Tablet I the birth goddesses, šassūrātu, help Mami bring the first humans to birth. The Plain follows the site's wording, "birth goddess." Enlil now calls her in to settle the future of human birth, the very thing that the noise came from.

p: The birth goddess sets each person's šīmtu, fate. Gilgamesh says she fixed death for humankind.
b: Bāniat šīmāti, "creator of destinies." A šīmtu is what is fixed for someone: lifespan, lot, death. In Gilgamesh the same goddess, Mammetum, "creator of destiny," decrees fates with the Anunnaki, and "when the gods created mankind, they allotted death to mankind" (Thompson). The Bible gives the days of each life into God's hand (Psalm 139:16; Psalm 31:15), and ties death to sin, not to a decree against overcrowding (Genesis 3:19; Romans 6:23).

p: SEAL restores "Set death for the people." If right, the gods gave humans a fixed death after the flood.
b: The start of the line is lost. SEAL restores it as [šuknī mūta] ana nišī, "[set death] for the people," and the next line as "[put a man] to sleep [in the grave]." The Plain leaves the restored words out, because no other copy or repeated line supports them. If the restoration is right, the poem says that a natural limit to life was set after the flood, alongside barrenness and infant death, as one more check on human numbers. Compare Genesis 6:3, "Their days will be 120 years," said before the flood, which many readers take as a limit on lifespan (see the note on Genesis 6:3).

p: After the flood the gods limit human numbers by barrenness, infant death and childless priestesses.
b: Enki proposes lasting limits instead of floods: women who cannot bear, the demon that takes babies, and orders of priestesses who must not have children. Tikva Frymer-Kensky argued that the problem behind plague, drought and flood was overpopulation, and that these measures are the poem's real answer to it. Others read the gods' complaint as about human rebellion or disorder. Heidel, writing before most of the poem was known, took the cause to be the noisy gatherings that kept Enlil awake.

a: women who give birth and women who do not
p: The gods make some women barren to keep numbers down. After the flood God says, "Be fruitful, grow many."
b: Conflicts: this is the sharpest contrast between the two flood stories. After the flood the gods of Atrahasis cut human births. The God of Genesis blesses: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1), and says it again: "As for you, be fruitful and grow many" (Genesis 9:7), repeating the blessing of creation (Genesis 1:28). In the Bible barrenness is a sorrow God often reverses (1 Samuel 1:5; Psalm 113:9), and the promise to Israel is that "no woman will lose her young or be unable to bear" (Exodus 23:26). Frymer-Kensky made this contrast central: Genesis rejects overpopulation as the problem.

p: A demon who snatches infants. The name is also given to the demoness Lamashtu.
b: Babylonians blamed infant deaths on demons, above all Lamashtu, a female demon said to seize babies and harm women in childbirth. Here the gods create such a power on purpose. Later Jewish lore told the same of Lilith, a name found once in the Bible for a night creature of the ruins (Isaiah 34:14, "Lilith, too, will settle there"). The Bible never says God made a demon to kill infants; Jesus says the little ones' angels "are always looking on the face of my Father in heaven" (Matthew 18:10).

a: Set up priestesses, the ugbabtu and the entu
p: Old Babylonian temples had orders of women who were not to have children. The poem explains them.
b: The entu was a high priestess (SEAL's gloss); the ugbabtu and igiṣītu were other priestesses. SEAL glosses ikkibu as "taboo": childbirth was forbidden to them. The poem gives these real institutions of its first hearers a reason in the age after the flood. Christian readers may compare celibacy, which the New Testament treats as a gift for the Lord's sake, not a limit on population (Matthew 19:12; 1 Corinthians 7:7, 32).

p: Qadištu is the Akkadian cousin of Hebrew qedeshah, often translated "temple prostitute."
b: The line is mostly restored: SEAL restores šugītu, and reads qadištu with a question mark from its last signs. Naditu women (12:77) lived as a cloister without children; SEAL glosses nadītu as a "fallow" (childless) woman. Qadištu, "holy woman," is the same word as Hebrew qedeshah (Genesis 38:21; Deuteronomy 23:17; Hosea 4:14). The KJV renders it "whore" at Deuteronomy 23:17, and other versions "cult prostitute." Here, though, the qadištu appears among consecrated women who must not bear children, not as a prostitute. This site renders the Hebrew "holy woman" (Genesis 38:21) and "shrine woman" (Deuteronomy 23:17); the Plain here follows Genesis 38:21, as at 4:36.

a: How we brought about the flood
p: The speaker of the closing lines is uncertain: Enlil, or the poet, praising Enki.
b: The last lines praise someone called "counselor of the gods" (12:95): probably Enki, whose counsel saved life. The speaker who says "we brought about the flood" and "I stirred up battle" may be Enlil, conceding Enki's wisdom; then the poet's own voice takes over with "this song" and "I have sung." The broken column before it (12:90) makes certainty impossible.

p: The poem ends as a hymn: the gods are to hear it and honor Enki's greatness.
b: The poem was not only a story but praise of a god, sung so that the Igigi would "take note" of his greatness. Babylonian scribes copied it in schools and temples. The Bible's songs of the flood praise the LORD: "At the Flood the LORD took his throne" (Psalm 29:10). Paul told people who worshiped such gods to turn "from these empty things to the God who lives" (Acts 14:15).

p: The singer calls all people to listen. Israel's songs call hearers to listen too, to a different story.
b: Uzammer šime'ā, "I have sung. Listen!" The poet claims a message for "all the people." Israel's teachers open the same way: "Listen, my people, to my teaching" (Psalm 78:1); "Listen closely, you heavens, and let me speak" (Deuteronomy 32:1). Moses' song tells of a God who "fathered" his people and "went into labor" with them (Deuteronomy 32:18), the claim the birth goddess makes in this poem. A Christian reader hears the call of Jesus: "Let anyone who has ears to hear listen" (Mark 4:9).

p: Babylonian poems were named by their first words. This is the title of Atrahasis.
b: Scribes named a work by its opening line, as Jews name the books of Moses (Bereshit, "In the beginning," for Genesis). Inūma ilū awīlum is the first line of the whole poem (1:1), whose meaning is debated; see the note there. Millard rendered it "When the gods, man-like."

p: The scribe counted 390 lines on this tablet and 1,245 in all. Scribes counted lines to protect the text.
b: The colophon says Tablet III had 390 lines and the three tablets 1,245. Counting lines let a later scribe check that nothing had been dropped. The Masoretes, the Jewish scribes who preserved the Hebrew Bible, did the same, counting verses and marking the middle of each book. The line counts also show how much of this poem is still lost: the present text of Tablet III has many gaps.

t: The scribe who copied the poem
p: Ipiq-Aya copied all three tablets at Sippar in the reign of Ammi-saduqa, king of Babylon.
b: Ipiq-Aya signs himself dub-sar tur, "junior scribe." He copied Tablet III, the last of the set, in the month Ayyaru (spring) of a year named for Ammi-saduqa's statues, which SEAL identifies as the king's twelfth year. Ammi-saduqa was the second-last king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, the dynasty of Hammurabi (Heidel); Millard dates this copy about 1630 BC. The tablets came from Sippar, the city of the sun god Shamash. These are the first real readers we can name: scribes in training and the temple and palace circles they served.

a: clasping a young goat to his chest
t: A year named for a statue
p: Babylonian years were named for a king's deeds, here two statues he gave to a temple.
b: Old Babylonian kings named each year after an event, often a gift to a god. This year name is mostly restored from the known list of Ammi-saduqa's years: he brought into the Eturkalamma temple a statue of himself holding a young goat (Sumerian máš) clasped to his chest, the pose of a worshiper bringing an offering, and another raising a hand in greeting. A statue in the temple let the king stand before his god in prayer. The Bible forbids images in worship (Exodus 20:4) and gives no king that role before God.
